cards.title: Start here · definition
cards.q: Where is your progress saved?
cards.a: In this browser, on this machine. It is not an account, and it does not leave the page.
cards.why: In this browser, on this machine. It is not an account, and it does not leave the page. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Start here · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “How to use this campus”?
cards.a: One file, a track order, and a way to know what you have finished.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Start here · definition
cards.q: What is the course trying to produce?
cards.a: Someone who can frame a task, choose a model and tools, evaluate the result, and hand the evidence to another person.
cards.why: Someone who can frame a task, choose a model and tools, evaluate the result, and hand the evidence to another person. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Start here · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “What you are learning to do”?
cards.a: The skill is judgment you can show, not a tour of product names.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Start here · definition
cards.q: Which field is the file another person can open later?
cards.a: The artifact. The trace explains how you got there. The metric says how it scored.
cards.why: The artifact. The trace explains how you got there. The metric says how it scored. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Start here · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Keep proof for every exercise”?
cards.a: Run, trace, metric, and artifact: four fields that make a lesson repeatable.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Start here · definition
cards.q: When is a tool allowed to send email on its own?
cards.a: It is not. Sending waits for a person, even if the draft looks correct.
cards.why: It is not. Sending waits for a person, even if the draft looks correct. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Start here · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Safety rules for every exercise”?
cards.a: Private data stays local until you have a reason to move it, and some actions always wait for a person.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Start here · definition
cards.q: Is an API key required to study?
cards.a: No. Add a local model or a hosted API only when an exercise needs a live call.
cards.why: No. Add a local model or a hosted API only when an exercise needs a live call. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Start here · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “What you need on your machine”?
cards.a: A current browser is enough to study. A local model is optional and comes later.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Start here · definition
cards.q: Why does fine-tuning come after evals?
cards.a: Because you need a measured failure of prompting and retrieval before training is a rational cost.
cards.why: Because you need a measured failure of prompting and retrieval before training is a rational cost. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Start here · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “How the tracks fit together”?
cards.a: Models, then prompting, then a way to ground and act, then proof that it worked.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: Why can a fluent answer still be false?
cards.a: Because the model is continuing likely text. Likelihood is not a citation.
cards.why: Because the model is continuing likely text. Likelihood is not a citation. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “A model predicts the next token”?
cards.a: Fluency is the product of a probability model. It is not a source of record.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: Why is 'about 0.75 words per token' not a budget?
cards.a: It is an English-prose average, not a count for your model, your language, or your code.
cards.why: It is an English-prose average, not a count for your model, your language, or your code. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Tokens are the unit of cost and context”?
cards.a: A token is a chunk of text, not a word, and every limit you hit is counted in tokens.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: Who shares the context window?
cards.a: The instructions, the retrieved or pasted sources, the conversation, and the tokens the model still has to write.
cards.why: The instructions, the retrieved or pasted sources, the conversation, and the tokens the model still has to write. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “The context window is one shared budget”?
cards.a: Instructions, retrieved text, the conversation, and the answer all spend the same token limit.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: Does a low temperature stop hallucinations?
cards.a: No. It reduces random variation. A likely-but-wrong token can still be the top choice.
cards.why: No. It reduces random variation. A likely-but-wrong token can still be the top choice. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Temperature is a sampling control”?
cards.a: Lower settings repeat likely tokens. Higher settings take more risks. Neither setting checks facts.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: What do you score instead of the model's confidence?
cards.a: Whether the answer matches a source, a tool result, or a known test case.
cards.why: Whether the answer matches a source, a tool result, or a known test case. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Hallucination is fluent text without evidence”?
cards.a: Catch it with sources, tools, and tests. Do not catch it by asking the model if it is sure.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: Where do tool results belong?
cards.a: In a tool message, separate from the user's request, so the model can see what the tool returned.
cards.why: In a tool message, separate from the user's request, so the model can see what the tool returned. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “System, user, and tool messages do different jobs”?
cards.a: Put standing rules in the system message. Put the task in the user message. Put tool results in tool messages.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: Why do you pin a model id?
cards.a: Because a family name hides version changes that move quality, cost, and safety.
cards.why: Because a family name hides version changes that move quality, cost, and safety. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Model families you will see in 2026 job posts”?
cards.a: Hire and design for a role, then pin an id. A family name is not a version.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: What should you try before you switch on a slower reasoning model?
cards.a: A fast model on a fixed set of examples, after the prompt and output shape are clear.
cards.why: A fast model on a fixed set of examples, after the prompt and output shape are clear. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Choose a reasoning model or a fast chat model”?
cards.a: Spend extra compute when the task needs a plan. Do not spend it on extraction you can score cheaply.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: What makes a done-check real?
cards.a: A person or a test can apply it to the output without asking the model whether it tried hard.
cards.why: A person or a test can apply it to the output without asking the model whether it tried hard. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Write the job, the input, and the done-check”?
cards.a: A prompt is a job description. If you cannot tell whether the answer succeeded, the prompt is not finished.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: Why validate in code if you asked for JSON?
cards.a: Because the model can still wrap it in prose, drop a bracket, or invent a key. The schema mode reduces that. It does not replace the check.
cards.why: Because the model can still wrap it in prose, drop a bracket, or invent a key. The schema mode reduces that. It does not replace the check. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Lock the output shape”?
cards.a: Ask for a structure, then validate it in code. Prose that looks like JSON is not JSON.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: Why include a refusal example?
cards.a: Because otherwise every example shows a successful extraction, and the model learns to fill gaps.
cards.why: Because otherwise every example shows a successful extraction, and the model learns to fill gaps. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Few-shot examples that do not leak”?
cards.a: Examples teach the pattern. They are also data you might not have permission to send.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: When is a fixed workflow the better design?
cards.a: When you can name the steps in advance and test each one. Choice belongs in a loop only when the next action depends on what came back.
cards.why: When you can name the steps in advance and test each one. Choice belongs in a loop only when the next action depends on what came back. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Split a hard task into steps you can test”?
cards.a: One prompt that plans, searches, calculates, and drafts is several jobs hiding in a paragraph.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: What is the revision allowed to change?
cards.a: Only the lines that failed the checklist.
cards.why: Only the lines that failed the checklist. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Critique the draft, then revise once”?
cards.a: A second pass helps when the critique is a checklist, not a request to 'make it better'.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: Why is the model not the security boundary?
cards.a: Because it is trained to follow instructions it reads. Code has to restrict tools, validate arguments, and gate side effects.
cards.why: Because it is trained to follow instructions it reads. Code has to restrict tools, validate arguments, and gate side effects. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Prompt injection is untrusted text that pretends to be an order”?
cards.a: Documents, web pages, and tool descriptions can carry instructions. Your system does not have to obey them.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: Why run the old passing cases after a prompt edit?
cards.a: Because the edit can fix the example you stared at and damage the rest.
cards.why: Because the edit can fix the example you stared at and damage the rest. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Change one thing, then score it”?
cards.a: A prompt edit without a before-and-after score is a new opinion.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: Does local mean more accurate?
cards.a: No. It means you control where the weights run and where the prompt goes. Accuracy is an eval result.
cards.why: No. It means you control where the weights run and where the prompt goes. Accuracy is an eval result. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Local models · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Run a model locally when the data should stay put”?
cards.a: Local is a privacy and latency choice. It is not automatically the more accurate choice.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: Where should a personal lab listen?
cards.a: On localhost. A model service bound to every network interface is a different, riskier setup.
cards.why: On localhost. A model service bound to every network interface is a different, riskier setup. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Local models · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Install a runner and call it on localhost”?
cards.a: Ollama and llama.cpp are the usual local runners. The smoke check is a local HTTP call or a CLI completion.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: Why not start with the largest model you can find?
cards.a: Because a model that does not fit does not run, and a model that barely fits leaves no room for context.
cards.why: Because a model that does not fit does not run, and a model that barely fits leaves no room for context. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Local models · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Pick a model size that fits in memory”?
cards.a: If the weights do not fit, the runner will swap, crash, or refuse. Start smaller than your pride.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: What does Q4 tell you by itself?
cards.a: That the weights were stored at about 4 bits. Not whether the model passes your tasks.
cards.why: That the weights were stored at about 4 bits. Not whether the model passes your tasks. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Local models · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Quantization trades precision for fit”?
cards.a: The weights are stored with fewer bits. You measure whether your tasks still pass.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: Does downloadable mean you may sell a product that hides the model inside?
cards.a: No. That depends on the license that came with those weights.
cards.why: No. That depends on the license that came with those weights. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Local models · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Read the license before you ship a weight”?
cards.a: Open weights are not one license. Some allow commercial use. Some restrict it. Some restrict use of the outputs for training.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: What should you check before you rewrite a prompt that 'suddenly failed'?
cards.a: That the runner is up and the model id matches the one in your last good artifact.
cards.why: That the runner is up and the model id matches the one in your last good artifact. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Local models · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Keep a smoke test you can rerun”?
cards.a: After a reboot, prove the runner is up before you debug the prompt.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: Which of the three belongs in git?
cards.a: Prompts and fixtures that contain no secrets and no private corpus. Not weights. Not private notes.
cards.why: Prompts and fixtures that contain no secrets and no private corpus. Not weights. Not private notes. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Local models · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Keep weights, prompts, and private data apart”?
cards.a: Different files, different backups, different permissions.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: What do you do if a key lands in a log?
cards.a: Revoke it, then fix the log. Keeping the key and editing one file is not enough if the log was copied.
cards.why: Revoke it, then fix the log. Keeping the key and editing one file is not enough if the log was copied. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: APIs and cost · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Call an API without putting the key in the repo”?
cards.a: The key lives in an environment or a secret store. The client reads it at runtime. Logs do not print it.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: What can a schema guarantee?
cards.a: Shape. Not truth, and not that an id exists in your corpus.
cards.why: Shape. Not truth, and not that an id exists in your corpus. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: APIs and cost · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Ask for structured output and check it”?
cards.a: Schema mode is a feature of the API. Your parser is still the gate.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: Why is an immediate retry of a 429 a mistake?
cards.a: The provider asked you to slow down. Immediate retries spend the same quota faster and can make the block longer.
cards.why: The provider asked you to slow down. Immediate retries spend the same quota faster and can make the block longer. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: APIs and cost · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Set timeouts, retries, and a rate-limit plan”?
cards.a: A hung call is a product bug. A retry storm is a bill.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: Why is cost per call the wrong product number?
cards.a: Because failed calls, retries, and human cleanup are part of the real cost of a successful task.
cards.why: Because failed calls, retries, and human cleanup are part of the real cost of a successful task. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: APIs and cost · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Read the bill in tokens, cache, and batch”?
cards.a: Cost is a property of the design. Input tokens, output tokens, and tool calls are the levers.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: What must stay constant when you swap providers?
cards.a: The tasks, the checks, and the fields you record. Otherwise you are comparing prompts, not providers.
cards.why: The tasks, the checks, and the fields you record. Otherwise you are comparing prompts, not providers. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: APIs and cost · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Compare providers on the same ten tasks”?
cards.a: Swap the client. Keep the fixture, the schema, and the scorecard.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: Name two fields that belong in a model-call log and one that does not.
cards.a: Belong: model id and token counts, or latency and status. Does not: the API key, or a private document you have no approval to store.
cards.why: Belong: model id and token counts, or latency and status. Does not: the API key, or a private document you have no approval to store. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: APIs and cost · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Log the call without logging the secret”?
cards.a: Keep the model id, the latency, the token counts, and a hash or id of the prompt. Drop the key and the raw private text unless you have a place to store it.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: When should the system refuse?
cards.a: When the retrieved passages do not contain the answer, even if the model could guess.
cards.why: When the retrieved passages do not contain the answer, even if the model could guess. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Retrieve when the answer has to come from a source”?
cards.a: Retrieval-augmented generation finds passages first, then asks the model to answer from those passages.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: Why is there no universal best chunk size?
cards.a: Because the right boundary is the structure of the document and the questions you ask, which you measure.
cards.why: Because the right boundary is the structure of the document and the questions you ask, which you measure. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Chunk documents so a citation can point at them”?
cards.a: Split on structure. Keep a stable id. Do not hunt for a magic token count.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: What do you re-embed when you change embedding models?
cards.a: The whole corpus. Old vectors are not comparable to new ones.
cards.why: The whole corpus. Old vectors are not comparable to new ones. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Search with keywords and with embeddings”?
cards.a: Embeddings find similar meaning. Keywords find the exact name. Hybrid search uses both.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: What failure can a reranker not repair?
cards.a: A first stage that never retrieved the right chunk.
cards.why: A first stage that never retrieved the right chunk. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Rerank a short list before you prompt”?
cards.a: Retrieve widely, then keep the few passages that actually answer.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: What makes a citation checkable?
cards.a: It names an id you retrieved and a place in that source a person can find.
cards.why: It names an id you retrieved and a place in that source a person can find. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Cite a passage a person can open”?
cards.a: A citation is an id and a span, not a confident tone.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: A fluent answer cites nothing and sounds right. Where do you look first?
cards.a: At whether any retrieved chunk contained the claim. If none did, the failure is retrieval or refusal, not prose style.
cards.why: At whether any retrieved chunk contained the claim. If none did, the failure is retrieval or refusal, not prose style. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Failure modes to test before you tune the prompt”?
cards.a: Wrong chunk, stale chunk, lost middle, and a corpus that never contained the fact.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: Why score retrieval separately from the answer?
cards.a: Because a wrong passage cannot be saved by the writer, and a right passage can still be ignored. The two failures have different fixes.
cards.why: Because a wrong passage cannot be saved by the writer, and a right passage can still be ignored. The two failures have different fixes. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Measure retrieval before you measure the answer”?
cards.a: Recall on the right chunk is a different number from whether the paragraph was helpful.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: What turns a model call into an agent?
cards.a: A loop that can call tools, observe results, and stop on a rule you set.
cards.why: A loop that can call tools, observe results, and stop on a rule you set. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “An agent is a loop with a stop rule”?
cards.a: The model may call a tool, read the result, and repeat, until an answer or a cap.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: Who enforces the schema, the model or your code?
cards.a: Your code. The model only proposes the call.
cards.why: Your code. The model only proposes the call. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Give every tool a name, a schema, and a handler”?
cards.a: The model proposes a call. Your code checks the arguments and runs the handler.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: Why an allowlist instead of a denylist?
cards.a: New tools stay unavailable until you classify them. A denylist treats silence as permission.
cards.why: New tools stay unavailable until you classify them. A denylist treats silence as permission. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Allow, deny, and ask a person”?
cards.a: Read-only tools can run inside the cap. Anything that leaves the machine waits.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: Is a vector store the same as the chat thread?
cards.a: No. The thread dies with the task. A store remains, and it needs a retention rule.
cards.why: No. The thread dies with the task. A store remains, and it needs a retention rule. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Decide what the agent is allowed to remember”?
cards.a: The thread, a file, and a store are different lifetimes. Pick one on purpose.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: What has to cross the boundary between two agents?
cards.a: A structured artifact, not an open-ended chat, plus a narrower tool list on each side.
cards.why: A structured artifact, not an open-ended chat, plus a narrower tool list on each side. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Add another agent only when the handoff is a real artifact”?
cards.a: Two agents that share a vague chat are one confused loop with extra cost.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: The summary says a file was not touched. The trace shows a write call. Which do you believe?
cards.a: The trace. Then you find out why the summary hid it.
cards.why: The trace. Then you find out why the summary hid it. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Read the trace, not the closing summary”?
cards.a: Every tool call, argument, result, and approval is a line you can reconstruct.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: Why is a calculator easier to retry than a send-email tool?
cards.a: A second calculation returns the same number. A second send delivers a second email.
cards.why: A second calculation returns the same number. A second send delivers a second email. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Make tool calls safe to retry, inside a sandbox”?
cards.a: A second run of the same call should not double-send, double-charge, or escape the folder.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: Is the MCP server the language model?
cards.a: No. The server exposes capabilities. The model runs in the host and asks the client to call the server.
cards.why: No. The server exposes capabilities. The model runs in the host and asks the client to call the server. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: MCP · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “MCP connects a model to tools you did not hard-code”?
cards.a: The Model Context Protocol is a standard way for an app to talk to a tool server.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: Where should a database password live?
cards.a: On the server, in its environment. Not in the prompt, and not in a tool description.
cards.why: On the server, in its environment. Not in the prompt, and not in a tool description. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: MCP · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Host, client, and server have different jobs”?
cards.a: The person uses the host. The client holds the session. The server does the work.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: Why is a resource still a safety issue if it cannot write?
cards.a: Because its text enters the model's context and can carry instructions. Read-only is not the same as trusted.
cards.why: Because its text enters the model's context and can carry instructions. Read-only is not the same as trusted. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: MCP · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Tools act, resources are read, prompts are templates”?
cards.a: Use the primitive that matches the risk.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: What does stdio mean for where the server runs?
cards.a: On the same machine, as a child process of the host, with the power of the environment you gave it.
cards.why: On the same machine, as a child process of the host, with the power of the environment you gave it. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: MCP · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Connect a local server over stdio”?
cards.a: The host starts a process and speaks MCP on its standard streams. The process is the trust boundary.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: Why is a tool description a safety boundary?
cards.a: Because it is inserted into the model's context. A hostile description is an instruction the model may follow.
cards.why: Because it is inserted into the model's context. A hostile description is an instruction the model may follow. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: MCP · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Consent, authentication, and untrusted servers”?
cards.a: A server you did not review can read what the host will hand it, and its tool text can steer the model.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: Does connecting an issue tracker via MCP remove the need to review the diff?
cards.a: No. It adds context. The change to the repo is still reviewed against tests and intent.
cards.why: No. It adds context. The change to the repo is still reviewed against tests and intent. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: MCP · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “How coding tools use MCP”?
cards.a: Editors and agents use MCP to reach issue trackers, browsers, docs, and internal APIs. The repo is still reviewed by a person.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · definition
cards.q: What is the result of a coding agent, the summary or the diff?
cards.a: The diff, plus the test command you ran. The summary is a claim about them.
cards.why: The diff, plus the test command you ran. The summary is a claim about them. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Coding agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “A coding agent edits a repository under rules”?
cards.a: It can read, propose a plan, change files, and run commands. Your rules say which of those happen alone.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · definition
cards.q: Why name a test in the goal?
cards.a: Because that command is the done-check. A green test is evidence. A summary is not.
cards.why: Because that command is the done-check. A green test is evidence. A summary is not. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Coding agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Give the agent the files and tests that matter”?
cards.a: A whole monorepo in the prompt is not context. It is noise.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · definition
cards.q: When is it reasonable to skip the written plan?
cards.a: When the change is small and you already named the file and the test. Not when the agent is still looking for the cause.
cards.why: When the change is small and you already named the file and the test. Not when the agent is still looking for the cause. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Coding agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Plan, edit, run, then stop”?
cards.a: A plan you can reject is cheaper than a pile of edits you have to unwind.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · definition
cards.q: The agent says the tests passed. What do you do?
cards.a: Run the named command and read the output. Check that the tests still assert the behavior you wanted.
cards.why: Run the named command and read the output. Check that the tests still assert the behavior you wanted. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Coding agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Review the diff and the tests”?
cards.a: Read the change as if a new teammate wrote it. Then run the same command they ran.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · definition
cards.q: Where does the deny list have to live to be real?
cards.a: In the tool permissions, not only in the prompt.
cards.why: In the tool permissions, not only in the prompt. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Coding agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Secrets, destructive git, and the network”?
cards.a: The expensive mistakes are not bad indentation.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · definition
cards.q: Who is responsible for an agent-written change that ships?
cards.a: The person who reviewed and merged it. The agent is not an author of record.
cards.why: The person who reviewed and merged it. The agent is not an author of record. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Coding agents · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Use a coding agent on a team without shipping junk”?
cards.a: Agree the permissions, the review, and what 'the agent did it' does not excuse.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: What makes an eval different from trying a prompt in a chat?
cards.a: The tasks stay fixed, the score is recorded, and a later change has to beat that record.
cards.why: The tasks stay fixed, the score is recorded, and a later change has to beat that record. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “An eval is a versioned test, not a feeling”?
cards.a: You cannot prefer a new prompt unless the same tasks were scored both times.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: Why not generate the whole set with a model and trust it?
cards.a: Because the generator's mistakes become the score. A person has to own the expected checks.
cards.why: Because the generator's mistakes become the score. A person has to own the expected checks. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Start with ten tasks you can explain”?
cards.a: A small set you trust beats a large set nobody can audit.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: Why keep cost beside quality?
cards.a: Because a gain that doubles spend or latency can be the wrong ship even when more answers are correct.
cards.why: Because a gain that doubles spend or latency can be the wrong ship even when more answers are correct. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Score quality, safety, latency, and cost together”?
cards.a: A change that raises quality and doubles the bill needs a decision, not a silent ship.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: What do you compare a judge model against before you trust it?
cards.a: A sample you scored yourself, on the same rubric.
cards.why: A sample you scored yourself, on the same rubric. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Use a model as a judge only with a rubric and an audit”?
cards.a: A judge model is a second system. It has its own failure rate.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: Why is a new embedding model not a free change?
cards.a: Because the vectors change. You rebuild the index and rescore retrieval, or you do not know what you shipped.
cards.why: Because the vectors change. You rebuild the index and rescore retrieval, or you do not know what you shipped. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Gate changes to the prompt, the model, and the index”?
cards.a: Each of those is a release. The tasks do not change in the same commit unless the task change is the point.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: What is the pass condition of a red-team task?
cards.a: That the system followed the rule: refusal, denial in the trace, or no secret in the output. Not that the model gave a clever reply.
cards.why: That the system followed the rule: refusal, denial in the trace, or no secret in the output. Not that the model gave a clever reply. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Put red-team cases in the set early”?
cards.a: You are checking your own system's boundaries, on inputs you control.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: What belongs in the scorecard besides the pass count?
cards.a: The pins — prompt, model, index — plus safety, latency or cost, regressions, and the gate result.
cards.why: The pins — prompt, model, index — plus safety, latency or cost, regressions, and the gate result. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Keep the scorecard next to the artifact”?
cards.a: A table you can reopen beats a screenshot of one good answer.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · definition
cards.q: Name one problem retrieval solves better than fine-tuning.
cards.a: Facts that change, or facts that must be cited from a source you can update without training.
cards.why: Facts that change, or facts that must be cited from a source you can update without training. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Fine-tune only after a measured failure of the cheaper fixes”?
cards.a: Prompt, schema, retrieval, and tools come first. Training is for a gap those did not close.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · definition
cards.q: What do you save after a LoRA run?
cards.a: The adapter, and a record of the base model id it attaches to. The adapter without the matching base is not a model.
cards.why: The adapter, and a record of the base model id it attaches to. The adapter without the matching base is not a model. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “LoRA trains a small adapter and leaves the base model frozen”?
cards.a: QLoRA does the same while the frozen base is stored in a quantized form.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · definition
cards.q: Why must eval tasks stay out of the training set?
cards.a: Because a high score would then mean the model saw the answers, not that it generalized.
cards.why: Because a high score would then mean the model saw the answers, not that it generalized. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Training data has a format, a license, and a leakage problem”?
cards.a: Examples teach the behavior. They also teach secrets you forgot were in the log.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · definition
cards.q: A adapter raises the average and fails a refusal task the base passed. Do you ship it?
cards.a: No, if refusal is in the gate. An average can rise while a safety regression lands.
cards.why: No, if refusal is in the gate. An average can rise while a safety regression lands. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Compare the adapter to the base model on the same tasks”?
cards.a: Keep the adapter only if the scorecard says so, including the tasks that used to pass.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · definition
cards.q: When is a larger base model a better answer than a fine-tune?
cards.a: When the larger model already passes the same tasks and you can afford it. You have not found a behavior the base cannot learn from context.
cards.why: When the larger model already passes the same tasks and you can afford it. You have not found a behavior the base cannot learn from context. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Prefer a prompt or a tool when that is the whole gap”?
cards.a: Most 'we should fine-tune' reviews end with a schema, a retrieval fix, or a smaller model.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Safety · definition
cards.q: What do you do with a tool that is not on the policy page?
cards.a: You do not enable it. The page is the allowlist.
cards.why: You do not enable it. The page is the allowlist. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Safety · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Write a one-page safety policy”?
cards.a: Name the data, the tools, the actions that need a person, and what you will not build.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · definition
cards.q: Name two stores that can retain a prompt.
cards.a: The provider, according to the settings on that key, and your own logs.
cards.why: The provider, according to the settings on that key, and your own logs. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Safety · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Decide retention before you log the prompt”?
cards.a: Prompts are often personal data. A debug log is a database.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · definition
cards.q: The model includes 'approved: true' in a tool argument. Does the handler run?
cards.a: No. Approval is a record your program stored before the call, tied to the exact arguments.
cards.why: No. Approval is a record your program stored before the call, tied to the exact arguments. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Safety · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “A person approves sends, payments, and deletes”?
cards.a: Drafting is not the same action as doing.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · definition
cards.q: What do you add to the eval after an incident?
cards.a: A task that reproduces the failure, with a pass condition that the new behavior holds.
cards.why: A task that reproduces the failure, with a pass condition that the new behavior holds. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Safety · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Write an incident note when the model misbehaves”?
cards.a: A short note beats a thread of screenshots.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · definition
cards.q: Is a jailbreak write-up a missing advanced chapter?
cards.a: No. Testing your own gates with cases you own is in scope. Instructions for breaking other systems are not.
cards.why: No. Testing your own gates with cases you own is in scope. Instructions for breaking other systems are not. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Safety · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “What this course will not help you do”?
cards.a: The boundary is part of the teaching.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: Where does the model name belong in the spec?
cards.a: After the job, the constraint, and the proof. It is a choice you can swap if the eval holds.
cards.why: After the job, the constraint, and the proof. It is a choice you can swap if the eval holds. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Product skills · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Name the job before you name the model”?
cards.a: A product sentence has a person, a job, and a constraint. The model is an implementation choice.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: Why write non-goals in the spec?
cards.a: Because an unnamed non-goal gets built as soon as a demo suggests it.
cards.why: Because an unnamed non-goal gets built as soon as a demo suggests it. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Product skills · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Write a one-page spec”?
cards.a: Problem, user, non-goals, success, risks, and the first milestone.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: Why is deflection alone a dangerous metric?
cards.a: The system can push work away, or answer wrongly, and the deflection count still rises.
cards.why: The system can push work away, or answer wrongly, and the deflection count still rises. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Product skills · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Share four numbers with engineering”?
cards.a: Quality, safety fails, latency, and cost per successful task.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: What should a 'wrong' answer let the person do?
cards.a: Open the citation and mark the failure so you can add it to the task set.
cards.why: Open the citation and mark the failure so you can add it to the task set. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Product skills · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Design the empty, slow, wrong, and unsafe states”?
cards.a: The model will hit all four. The interface should say what happened.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: What has to be true before the limited release?
cards.a: The gate passes on the frozen tasks, the audience is named, and you can turn the feature off.
cards.why: The gate passes on the frozen tasks, the audience is named, and you can turn the feature off. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Product skills · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Ship a prototype, then an eval, then a limited release”?
cards.a: A limited release has a named audience, a kill switch, and a date you will read the scorecard.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: Why is a smooth spoken answer a higher bar than a written one?
cards.a: Because the person cannot scan a citation while the sentence is already being said. The transcript and the handoff have to carry the check.
cards.why: Because the person cannot scan a citation while the sentence is already being said. The transcript and the handoff have to carry the check. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.title: Product skills · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Add voice only when latency and handoff are designed”?
cards.a: Speech recognition and speech synthesis are models with their own failure modes. They do not replace the eval.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.title: Capstone · definition
cards.q: What makes this small enough?
cards.a: A corpus you already may use, ten tasks, citations, at most one read-only tool, and no side effects.
cards.why: A corpus you already may use, ten tasks, citations, at most one read-only tool, and no side effects. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Choose a capstone you can finish on your own notes”?
cards.a: A folder you are allowed to use, questions you wrote, citations, and one read-only tool.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · definition
cards.q: Why write acceptance tests before the prompt?
cards.a: So the tests describe the job, not the last output you liked.
cards.why: So the tests describe the job, not the last output you liked. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Write the acceptance tests before the prompt”?
cards.a: If a test is awkward to write, the capstone is still too vague.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · definition
cards.q: What does a build-log entry contain?
cards.a: What changed, the score, where the artifact is, and the next change. Enough to repeat or to revert.
cards.why: What changed, the score, where the artifact is, and the next change. Enough to repeat or to revert. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Keep a build log as you go”?
cards.a: Each entry is a run, a trace pointer, a metric, and an artifact.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · definition
cards.q: Why include a task you still fail?
cards.a: Because the scorecard is evidence, and a perfect live demo without a remaining failure is usually a choice of questions.
cards.why: Because the scorecard is evidence, and a perfect live demo without a remaining failure is usually a choice of questions. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Demo the capstone in ten minutes”?
cards.a: Show a pass, a refusal, the trace, and the scorecard. Do not show a tour of the code.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · definition
cards.q: Can a capstone be complete if the gate fails?
cards.a: Yes, if the tasks, the trace, the policy, and the decision not to ship are all written down.
cards.why: Yes, if the tasks, the trace, the policy, and the decision not to ship are all written down. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · why
cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Decide the next change from the scorecard”?
cards.a: The capstone is finished when you can defend the gate, including a gate that says not yet.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Glossary · definition

cards.why: The set you show is the behavior you are sampling from.

cards.title: Prompting · why

cards.why: An open rewrite can fix one line and damage the rest.

cards.title: APIs and cost · why

cards.why: Cost is a product constraint. Surprise spend is a missing check.

cards.why: A retry without a cap is a bill you did not approve.

cards.q: In “The context window is one shared budget”, what should you keep from the note “Long context is not the same as attention”?
cards.a: A model with a large window can still miss a fact buried in the middle. If the fact matters, retrieve it and place it where the instruction says to look.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “The context window is one shared budget”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Sketch a budget for a task you care about: a percentage for rules, for source text, for the user message, and for the answer. The four parts must add to 100.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Temperature is a sampling control” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Lower settings repeat likely tokens. Higher settings take more risks. Neither setting checks facts.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: What does “Temperature is a sampling control” argue at the outset?
cards.a: After the model scores possible next tokens, a sampler chooses one. Temperature reshapes those scores. Low temperature, including zero where the API allows it, sticks to the most likely tokens. Higher temperature lets less likely tokens through.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Temperature is a sampling control” add?
cards.a: Related knobs, such as top-p, cut the tail of the distribution before sampling. You do not need the math to use them. You need a rule for which tasks may vary.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: What does “Temperature is a sampling control” add after those claims?
cards.a: Temperature does not turn a model into a database, and temperature zero is not a promise of bit-identical output across hardware, batching, or model updates.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Temperature is a sampling control”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Run one factual extraction twice at low temperature and twice at a high temperature, if you have any model available. If you do not, write the setting you will use for scored tasks and the setting you will refuse to use.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Hallucination is fluent text without evidence” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Catch it with sources, tools, and tests. Do not catch it by asking the model if it is sure.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: What does “Hallucination is fluent text without evidence” argue at the outset?
cards.a: In this course a hallucination is an answer that reads well and is not grounded in a source you can check. The model may invent a citation, a function, a date, or a confident 'yes'.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Hallucination is fluent text without evidence” add?
cards.a: Asking 'are you sure?' often produces another fluent paragraph. Confidence language is not a metric. Score the evidence.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: In “Hallucination is fluent text without evidence”, what should you keep from the note “Fake citations”?
cards.a: A bibliography the model typed is not a citation. A citation names an id in your corpus and a span a person can find.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Hallucination is fluent text without evidence”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write three questions whose correct answer is 'the sources do not say'. You will use them when you build retrieval.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “System, user, and tool messages do different jobs” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Put standing rules in the system message. Put the task in the user message. Put tool results in tool messages.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: What does “System, user, and tool messages do different jobs” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Chat APIs send a list of messages, not one blob. The roles are a contract with the model and with the software around it.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: What further claim does “System, user, and tool messages do different jobs” add?
cards.a: Some providers rename 'system' to 'developer' or split policy from instructions. Read the API you are calling. The job split stays the same: standing rules, this turn's task, and tool results are not the same channel.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “System, user, and tool messages do different jobs”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Rewrite a messy prompt you have used into three boxes: standing rules, this turn's task, and data. If a sentence could be data that contains instructions, mark it as data.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Model families you will see in 2026 job posts” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Hire and design for a role, then pin an id. A family name is not a version.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: What does “Model families you will see in 2026 job posts” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Posts in 2025 and 2026 rarely ask you to recite a parameter count. They ask which model you would call, how you would swap it, and how you would know the swap worked. Group the catalog by job, then check the vendor's current model card before you depend on a name.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: In “Model families you will see in 2026 job posts”, what should you keep from the note “Currency”?
cards.a: This table is a map of categories as of October 2026, not a shopping list. Model ids move. Your artifact should name the id you called and the date.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Model families you will see in 2026 job posts”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Pick a task you might actually run. Choose a role from the table and write one sentence on why the neighboring role is the wrong default.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Choose a reasoning model or a fast chat model” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Spend extra compute when the task needs a plan. Do not spend it on extraction you can score cheaply.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · definition
cards.q: What does “Choose a reasoning model or a fast chat model” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A reasoning model spends more tokens, and often more time, before it returns the answer you see. That helps on planning, difficult code, and problems where a wrong first guess is expensive. It is a poor default for 'pull these four fields out of this invoice' if a smaller, faster model already passes your tests.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Choose a reasoning model or a fast chat model” add?
cards.a: Do not chain a reasoning model behind every button in a product because a demo looked thoughtful. Latency is part of the product. School 09 turns this comparison into a gate.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: How models work · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Choose a reasoning model or a fast chat model”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Describe two tasks side by side: one that deserves a reasoning model and one that does not. Name the metric that would change your mind.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Vaswani et al., 2017. Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762.

cards.title: Prompting · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Write the job, the input, and the done-check” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A prompt is a job description. If you cannot tell whether the answer succeeded, the prompt is not finished.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: What does “Write the job, the input, and the done-check” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Start with three lines, in this order. Job: what the model must produce. Input: what it will receive. Done: the check a person or a program can apply without asking the model how it feels.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Write the job, the input, and the done-check” add?
cards.a: 'Make this better' fails the done-check. Better according to whom, measured how? Replace it with a change a reviewer can mark pass or fail.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Write the job, the input, and the done-check”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Take a prompt you have actually used. Rewrite it as job, input, and done. If you cannot write the done line, the task is not specified yet.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Prompting · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Lock the output shape” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Ask for a structure, then validate it in code. Prose that looks like JSON is not JSON.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: What does “Lock the output shape” argue at the outset?
cards.a: If the next step is code, the model must return a shape the code can parse. Use the provider's structured-output or JSON-schema mode when it exists. When it does not, still validate and reject.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Lock the output shape” add?
cards.a: Tables for a human reader are a different contract: column names, a maximum number of rows, and a rule for missing cells. Write that contract above the table, not in a hope that the model will infer it.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Lock the output shape”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write a schema for a task with three fields. Include one field that has a closed set of values. Note how you will reject a response that adds a fourth field.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Prompting · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Few-shot examples that do not leak” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Examples teach the pattern. They are also data you might not have permission to send.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: What does “Few-shot examples that do not leak” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Two or three examples beat a paragraph of adjectives. Each example needs the same shape as the real task: input, then the output you want, including a refusal example if refusal is correct sometimes.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: In “Few-shot examples that do not leak”, what should you keep from the note “Examples are instructions”?
cards.a: A model will imitate secrets, tone, and mistakes in the examples. A sloppy example teaches a sloppy format.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: Prompting · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Few-shot examples that do not leak”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write two synthetic examples for the schema in the previous lesson, plus one example whose correct output refuses to invent a missing field.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Prompting · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Split a hard task into steps you can test” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: One prompt that plans, searches, calculates, and drafts is several jobs hiding in a paragraph.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: What does “Split a hard task into steps you can test” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Decomposition means you name the intermediate results. Each result has a check. You can still send them in one call, or you can use a workflow. The win is the same: a failure has an address.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Split a hard task into steps you can test” add?
cards.a: Do not add a step because a diagram looked mature. Add a step when a single call fails in a way you can name. If classification is already perfect on your examples, it does not need its own model.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: In “Split a hard task into steps you can test”, what should you keep from the note “Workflows versus agents”?
cards.a: A fixed sequence is a workflow. A loop that chooses tools is an agent. Prefer the workflow until you can show that the next step depends on the previous result in a way you cannot write down.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: Prompting · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Split a hard task into steps you can test”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Take a task you would have put in one prompt. Split it into at most four steps. Write the input and output of each step in a single line.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Prompting · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Critique the draft, then revise once” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A second pass helps when the critique is a checklist, not a request to 'make it better'.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: What does “Critique the draft, then revise once” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A critique-revise pair is two jobs. The critique marks the draft against the done-check. The revision may change only the lines that failed. If you let the revision rewrite freely, you lose the parts that were already correct.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Critique the draft, then revise once” add?
cards.a: Cap this at one revision. A loop of critiques without a score is how you spend tokens to wander. If the checklist still fails, record the failure and stop.
