cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Critique the draft, then revise once”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write a three-item checklist for a writing task you care about. Make each item pass or fail, with no middle.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Prompting · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Prompt injection is untrusted text that pretends to be an order” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Documents, web pages, and tool descriptions can carry instructions. Your system does not have to obey them.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: What does “Prompt injection is untrusted text that pretends to be an order” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Prompt injection happens when text the model is reading — a web page, a PDF, an email, a tool description — contains instructions aimed at the model. The text might say to ignore the standing rules, reveal a secret, or call a tool. The model is not a security boundary. The software around it is.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: In “Prompt injection is untrusted text that pretends to be an order”, what should you keep from the note “What this lesson is not”?
cards.a: It is a recognition and testing lesson. It does not include payloads or bypass techniques.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Prompt injection is untrusted text that pretends to be an order” add?
cards.a: Indirect injection is the case you will meet in products: the user is honest, and the document they asked you to read is not. Treat retrieved text as data even when your own user is trusted.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Prompt injection is untrusted text that pretends to be an order”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Add one test case to your future eval notes: a source paragraph that tells the model to ignore the standing rules and invent a decision. Write the output you will mark as a failure.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Prompting · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Change one thing, then score it” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A prompt edit without a before-and-after score is a new opinion.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Prompting · definition
cards.q: What does “Change one thing, then score it” argue at the outset?
cards.a: When a result is wrong, change one variable. The instruction, the examples, the model, the temperature, or the retrieved text. Not all of them. Save the previous prompt as an artifact so you can return.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Change one thing, then score it” add?
cards.a: The last step is the one people skip. A prompt that fixes one row and breaks three is not an improvement. School 09 scales this to a set.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Prompting · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Change one thing, then score it”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Invent one failing row and one passing row for a prompt you wrote in 02-01. Note which single knob you would turn first.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Local models · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Run a model locally when the data should stay put” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Local is a privacy and latency choice. It is not automatically the more accurate choice.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: What does “Run a model locally when the data should stay put” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A local model runs on hardware you control. The prompt does not leave the machine, unless the software you wrapped around it sends it somewhere. That is the reason to prefer local for private notes, drafts of unreleased work, and air-gapped labs.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Run a model locally when the data should stay put” add?
cards.a: Accuracy is a separate question. A small local model can lose to a frontier API on hard reasoning and still be the right tool, because the task is simple enough and the data cannot move. Measure both. Do not treat 'local' as a moral category or 'cloud' as one.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Run a model locally when the data should stay put”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write one task that must stay on the machine and one task you would send to an API if the data were allowed to move. Name the reason in a clause, not a slogan.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Local models · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Install a runner and call it on localhost” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Ollama and llama.cpp are the usual local runners. The smoke check is a local HTTP call or a CLI completion.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: What does “Install a runner and call it on localhost” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Two common runners in 2026 are Ollama, which gives you a local service and a simple CLI, and llama.cpp, which runs GGUF weights with fine control over hardware. LM Studio and MLX on Apple silicon are other local options. vLLM is what teams use when they serve an open model to many callers. You do not need all of them.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: In “Install a runner and call it on localhost”, what should you keep from the note “No runner yet”?
cards.a: Keep going. Later practices accept a written plan in place of a live call. Do not create an API key just to finish a local-model lesson.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: Local models · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Install a runner and call it on localhost”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: If a runner is installed, save the tag list or the CLI's model list. If not, write the runner you will install and the exact check you will use to prove it is up.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Local models · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Pick a model size that fits in memory” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: If the weights do not fit, the runner will swap, crash, or refuse. Start smaller than your pride.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: What does “Pick a model size that fits in memory” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Memory is the constraint, not the slogan on the model card. A quantized 7B or 8B instruct model is a common first fit on a 16 GB laptop. Machines with 8 GB should start smaller. A 32 GB machine can try a larger quantized model after the small one has a smoke test.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Pick a model size that fits in memory” add?
cards.a: These are starting points, not laws. The same parameter count at a different quantization, context length, or runtime will use a different amount of memory. Watch the runner's reported memory and your system's pressure.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: What does “Pick a model size that fits in memory” add after those claims?
cards.a: Apple silicon uses unified memory. A discrete NVIDIA GPU uses its own memory, and the rest of the machine does not automatically extend it. CPU-only runs work and are slow. Slow is acceptable for a lesson. It is a product decision later.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Pick a model size that fits in memory”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write your memory budget and the first model class you will try. Include the sentence you will use if it does not fit: which smaller model you fall back to.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Local models · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Quantization trades precision for fit” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: The weights are stored with fewer bits. You measure whether your tasks still pass.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: What does “Quantization trades precision for fit” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Full-precision weights are large. Quantization stores those numbers in fewer bits so the model fits in memory and reads faster. GGUF is the file format llama.cpp and many local runners expect. You will see labels such as Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, and Q8_0. The digit is the bit budget. It is not a quality score.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Quantization trades precision for fit” add?
cards.a: A more aggressive quantization is smaller and more likely to damage reasoning, names, and tight formats. The only way to know is to run your fixture on two quantizations of the same model. If both pass, keep the smaller one. If the smaller one drops fields, step up or change models.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: In “Quantization trades precision for fit”, what should you keep from the note “Words that get confused”?
cards.a: Quantization changes how an existing model is stored. LoRA, in School 10, trains a small adapter. They are different tools and people mix the names in job posts. You should not.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: Local models · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Quantization trades precision for fit”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: In one paragraph, explain quantization to a teammate who thinks it means 'the model got smarter'. Include the measurement you would show them.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Local models · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Read the license before you ship a weight” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Open weights are not one license. Some allow commercial use. Some restrict it. Some restrict use of the outputs for training.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: What does “Read the license before you ship a weight” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A file you can download is not a file you can embed in a product. Model licenses differ: permissive licenses, licenses with an acceptable-use policy, and licenses that require a separate commercial grant above a size or revenue line. Read the license that shipped with the weights you pulled, not a blog summary of the family.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Read the license before you ship a weight”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Choose one open model you might run. Write the license name and one thing that license does not automatically let you do. If you cannot find the license, write 'not found' and do not treat the model as cleared.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Local models · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Keep a smoke test you can rerun” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: After a reboot, prove the runner is up before you debug the prompt.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: What does “Keep a smoke test you can rerun” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Half of 'the model got worse' is a runner that did not start, a disk that filled, or a different model tag than yesterday. A smoke test is cheaper than that confusion.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Keep a smoke test you can rerun” add?
cards.a: Run this after install, after reboot, and after you pull a new model. Save the result with the date. Five lines is enough.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Keep a smoke test you can rerun”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write the four checks as commands or button-presses for your runner. Leave a blank line under each for the last result.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Local models · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Keep weights, prompts, and private data apart” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Different files, different backups, different permissions.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Local models · definition
cards.q: What does “Keep weights, prompts, and private data apart” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Weights are large, replaceable, and often re-downloadable. Prompts are small and are the thing you version. Private notes are neither weights nor prompts. Mixing them in one folder is how a zip of 'the lab' leaks a journal or how a cleanup script deletes the only copy of a prompt.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Local models · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Keep weights, prompts, and private data apart”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Draw three boxes — weights, prompts, private data — and write the folder or setting you will use for each. Circle the one you will never commit.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: APIs and cost · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Call an API without putting the key in the repo” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: The key lives in an environment or a secret store. The client reads it at runtime. Logs do not print it.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: What does “Call an API without putting the key in the repo” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A hosted model is a metered remote service. The API key is a password that spends money and may be tied to your data-retention settings. Treat it that way.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Call an API without putting the key in the repo”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write the three places your key must never appear: a filename, a log field, and a chat surface you actually use. If you do not have a key, write the rule anyway.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: APIs and cost · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Ask for structured output and check it” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Schema mode is a feature of the API. Your parser is still the gate.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: What does “Ask for structured output and check it” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Hosted APIs in 2026 generally offer a way to constrain output: JSON schema, tool definitions, or a response format flag. Use it for anything a program will read. Then parse and validate. On failure, record the raw body, retry once with the validator message, and stop.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Ask for structured output and check it” add?
cards.a: Structured output does not make the values true. A schema can require `source_id` to be a string and still receive an id you do not have. Check membership against the ids you sent.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Ask for structured output and check it”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: List the three checks you would run on the decision schema from the prompting track. Mark which ones a JSON schema cannot do alone.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: APIs and cost · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Set timeouts, retries, and a rate-limit plan” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A hung call is a product bug. A retry storm is a bill.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: What does “Set timeouts, retries, and a rate-limit plan” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Every client needs a timeout. Choose it from the user's patience, not from hope. A chat answer and an overnight batch do not share a timeout.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Set timeouts, retries, and a rate-limit plan” add?
cards.a: Timeouts also bound runaway reasoning models. If the product cannot wait, do not call a model that might think for a minute. Fall back or tell the person the job is still running.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Set timeouts, retries, and a rate-limit plan”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: For a task you have in mind, write the timeout, the maximum retries, and one error you will not retry.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: APIs and cost · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Read the bill in tokens, cache, and batch” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Cost is a property of the design. Input tokens, output tokens, and tool calls are the levers.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: What does “Read the bill in tokens, cache, and batch” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Most hosted prices are per token, with input cheaper than output, and with extra rates for reasoning tokens, large context, or specialized tools. Read the current price page when you estimate. Do not memorize a number from this course.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Read the bill in tokens, cache, and batch” add?
cards.a: Track cost per successful task, not cost per call. A cheap call that fails and gets retried by a person is not cheap.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Read the bill in tokens, cache, and batch”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Sketch a one-line estimate: input tokens, output cap, and number of calls for one successful task. Leave the currency blank until you read the price page, and write the date you will check it.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: APIs and cost · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Compare providers on the same ten tasks” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Swap the client. Keep the fixture, the schema, and the scorecard.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: What does “Compare providers on the same ten tasks” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A provider comparison is an eval with more than one client. The tasks, the expected checks, and the recorded fields stay identical: quality, safety fails, latency, and cost. Changing the prompt to flatter one provider invalidates the comparison.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Compare providers on the same ten tasks” add?
cards.a: Also record the operational facts: data-retention default, region, whether prompt caching exists, and how structured output is spelled in that API. A model that scores well and retains data you cannot retain is not a win.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: In “Compare providers on the same ten tasks”, what should you keep from the note “Multi-provider is a maintenance cost”?
cards.a: Two clients means two schemas, two failure modes, and two invoices. Take that on when the eval or the constraint demands it, not because an architecture diagram had a second box.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: APIs and cost · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Compare providers on the same ten tasks”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write the header row of a comparison sheet: provider, model id, pass count, safety fails, median latency, cost for the ten, retention note. Fill 'not run' if you have not called anyone.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: APIs and cost · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Log the call without logging the secret” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Keep the model id, the latency, the token counts, and a hash or id of the prompt. Drop the key and the raw private text unless you have a place to store it.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: APIs and cost · definition
cards.q: What does “Log the call without logging the secret” argue at the outset?
cards.a: You will need logs when a call fails. You do not need the Authorization header, and you often do not need the full prompt if the prompt contains private text. Design the log line before the first incident.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Log the call without logging the secret” add?
cards.a: Staging and production keys differ. A log from staging should be obvious, so a debug session does not 'just this once' use the production key against a toy prompt that contains real data.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: APIs and cost · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Log the call without logging the secret”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write one log line, with fake values, that would be safe to paste into a ticket. Then write the same event the unsafe way, and cross it out.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Retrieval · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Retrieve when the answer has to come from a source” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Retrieval-augmented generation finds passages first, then asks the model to answer from those passages.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: What does “Retrieve when the answer has to come from a source” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Use retrieval when the words that justify the answer live in a corpus: your notes, a policy set, a code repository, a product manual. Do not use it to decorate a question the model can already refuse, or to pretend you have searched the live web when you have not.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Retrieve when the answer has to come from a source” add?
cards.a: If you skip the third, the model will fill the gap and your citations will make the invention look official.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Retrieve when the answer has to come from a source”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Name a corpus you actually have, even a folder of ten notes. Write two questions the corpus can answer and one it cannot. The third is a required test, not a trick.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Chunk documents so a citation can point at them” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Split on structure. Keep a stable id. Do not hunt for a magic token count.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: What does “Chunk documents so a citation can point at them” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A chunk is the unit you retrieve and the unit you cite. If a chunk mixes three topics, the citation cannot tell the reader which one supported the sentence. If a chunk splits a procedure in half, the answer will miss a step.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Chunk documents so a citation can point at them” add?
cards.a: Start with a boring size that respects headings. Change it when the eval says the right fact is split or buried, not when a blog names a different number.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Chunk documents so a citation can point at them”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Take one real page and mark the chunk boundaries with a pencil. Write an id scheme, such as `note-14#setup`. Check that each chunk still makes sense alone.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Search with keywords and with embeddings” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Embeddings find similar meaning. Keywords find the exact name. Hybrid search uses both.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: What does “Search with keywords and with embeddings” argue at the outset?
cards.a: An embedding model turns text into a vector so you can search by similarity. It is not the chat model. Pin the embedding model the same way you pin a chat model. If you change it, re-embed the corpus. Mixed vectors in one index are silent nonsense.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Search with keywords and with embeddings” add?
cards.a: Keyword search, such as BM25, finds the rare exact string: an error code, a function name, a SKU. Embeddings miss those and find paraphrases. Hybrid retrieval runs both and merges the lists. That combination is the ordinary 2026 default, not an advanced trick.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Search with keywords and with embeddings”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write one query that needs an exact string and one that is a paraphrase of a heading in your corpus. Note which search should find each.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Rerank a short list before you prompt” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Retrieve widely, then keep the few passages that actually answer.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: What does “Rerank a short list before you prompt” argue at the outset?
cards.a: The first-stage search is tuned to recall: do not miss the right chunk. That list is too long and too noisy to paste into the prompt. A reranker, or a simple second score, reads the question and each candidate and keeps the best few.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Rerank a short list before you prompt” add?
cards.a: Reranking is cheaper than stuffing thirty chunks into a frontier model, and it reduces the chance that a vaguely related paragraph outshouts the real one. It does not create a passage you failed to retrieve. If the right chunk was never in the candidate list, fix the first stage.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Rerank a short list before you prompt”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: For one question, list five candidate chunks you would expect, in the order a person would keep them. Circle the ones you would actually paste into the prompt.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Cite a passage a person can open” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A citation is an id and a span, not a confident tone.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: What does “Cite a passage a person can open” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Require the answer to name the chunk ids it used. Render those ids as labels a person can click or open. If the model cites an id that was not in the retrieved set, drop the sentence or fail the answer. That check is code.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Cite a passage a person can open” add?
cards.a: Quote the supporting span when the decision is risky. A paraphrase with a footnote is easier to drift. The quote is the artifact. The paraphrase is the interface.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: In “Cite a passage a person can open”, what should you keep from the note “The model will invent ids”?
cards.a: That is normal. The repair is the membership check, plus an eval row where a fake id is the wrong answer.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Cite a passage a person can open”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write the citation line you want for one chunk in your corpus: id, title path, and span. Then write the rule your code will apply if the model cites anything else.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Failure modes to test before you tune the prompt” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Wrong chunk, stale chunk, lost middle, and a corpus that never contained the fact.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: What does “Failure modes to test before you tune the prompt” argue at the outset?
cards.a: When a grounded assistant is wrong, look at the pipeline in order. Prompt edits are last.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Failure modes to test before you tune the prompt” add?
cards.a: Agentic retrieval — letting a model search again and again — comes after this table is mostly green. A loop on a broken index spends tokens to miss the same chunk.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Failure modes to test before you tune the prompt”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write one fixture row for each row of the table, using your corpus or a synthetic page. You only need the question, the expected chunk id or the expected refusal, and the failure name.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Measure retrieval before you measure the answer” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Recall on the right chunk is a different number from whether the paragraph was helpful.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: What does “Measure retrieval before you measure the answer” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Build a small labeled set: question, and the chunk ids that must appear. Run retrieval alone. Report how often the right id is in the top 5, and how often it is the one you would have pasted. That is the retrieval metric.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Measure retrieval before you measure the answer” add?
cards.a: Only then score the written answer. If retrieval recall is poor, an answer score mostly measures luck and invention. Fix the index, the embedding model, the keywords, or the chunks. Then rescore.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · definition
cards.q: In “Measure retrieval before you measure the answer”, what should you keep from the note “Freshness”?
cards.a: Add the source's updated time and the index time to the artifact. A perfect score on last month's export is not a score on today's policy.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Retrieval · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Measure retrieval before you measure the answer”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Create five labeled questions in the format above. If you cannot name a must_include id, you do not have a retrieval test yet. You have a vibe.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “An agent is a loop with a stop rule” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: The model may call a tool, read the result, and repeat, until an answer or a cap.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: What does “An agent is a loop with a stop rule” argue at the outset?
cards.a: An agent is not a persona and not a long prompt. It is a loop. The model looks at the goal and the observations so far, then either calls a tool or returns a final answer. Your program runs the tool, appends the observation, and asks again.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: What further claim does “An agent is a loop with a stop rule” add?
cards.a: Worked shape: the goal is 'what is 15 percent of 80, and is that above 10?' The only tool is `calc`. The model calls `calc`, reads 12, and answers. If `calc` errors, the agent says it could not compute. It does not invent 12 because 12 is plausible.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “An agent is a loop with a stop rule”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write a goal, the only tools you would allow, the step cap, and the exact sentence for a cap hit. Save it as the artifact for this lesson.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Give every tool a name, a schema, and a handler” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: The model proposes a call. Your code checks the arguments and runs the handler.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: What does “Give every tool a name, a schema, and a handler” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A tool the model can call needs a name, a description of when to use it, a JSON schema for the arguments, and a handler you wrote. The description is read by the model. The schema is enforced by your code.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Give every tool a name, a schema, and a handler”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write a schema for one read-only tool you would actually want, with one required field and additional properties forbidden.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Allow, deny, and ask a person” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Read-only tools can run inside the cap. Anything that leaves the machine waits.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: What does “Allow, deny, and ask a person” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Write an allowlist. The complement is denied. A denylist of 'dangerous' tools fails the day you add a new tool and forget to classify it.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Allow, deny, and ask a person” add?
cards.a: Approval is a UI, not a sentence in the prompt. The person sees the tool name and the arguments and chooses yes or no. A timeout is a no. A missing approver is a no.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: In “Allow, deny, and ask a person”, what should you keep from the note “The model will argue”?
cards.a: An observation that says the user already approved is not an approval. Approval is a record your program wrote before the handler ran.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: Agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Allow, deny, and ask a person”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Sort five actions you might automate into allow, draft-only, and ask. Include at least one ask.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Decide what the agent is allowed to remember” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: The thread, a file, and a store are different lifetimes. Pick one on purpose.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: What does “Decide what the agent is allowed to remember” argue at the outset?
cards.a: People say 'memory' and mean three mechanisms.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Decide what the agent is allowed to remember” add?
cards.a: Do not silently write the conversation into a long-term store. That store becomes personal data. Say what is saved, for how long, and how a person deletes it. Inside one task, prefer the thread plus an explicit artifact file.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: What does “Decide what the agent is allowed to remember” add after those claims?
cards.a: Trim the thread on purpose when it grows: keep the goal, the last observations, and the artifact ids. Dumping every token back in is how you blow the context window and the bill.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Decide what the agent is allowed to remember”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: For the agent note you wrote in 06-01, say what is kept only for the task and what, if anything, is written to a file. Name the file.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Add another agent only when the handoff is a real artifact” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Two agents that share a vague chat are one confused loop with extra cost.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: What does “Add another agent only when the handoff is a real artifact” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A second agent is justified when it has a different tool allowlist or a different job, and it receives a structured artifact from the first. A researcher that may only search, handing a citation list to a writer that may only draft, is a real split. Two personas in one transcript is not.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Add another agent only when the handoff is a real artifact” add?
cards.a: If you cannot name the artifact that crosses the boundary, keep one agent.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Add another agent only when the handoff is a real artifact”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Either describe a handoff schema between two roles, or write 'one agent' and the reason a second role would be fake.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Read the trace, not the closing summary” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Every tool call, argument, result, and approval is a line you can reconstruct.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: What does “Read the trace, not the closing summary” argue at the outset?
cards.a: The agent's final paragraph is a claim about what it did. The trace is what it did. When they disagree, believe the trace and fix the summary.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Read the trace, not the closing summary” add?
cards.a: This is also how you debug a loop that 'got stuck'. The trace shows the repeated call. The summary says it explored thoroughly.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Read the trace, not the closing summary”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write a four-line trace for a task with one tool call and one stop. Include the cap counters.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Make tool calls safe to retry, inside a sandbox” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A second run of the same call should not double-send, double-charge, or escape the folder.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Agents · definition
cards.q: What does “Make tool calls safe to retry, inside a sandbox” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Networks fail after the side effect and before the response. If your client retries, the tool runs twice unless the handler is idempotent. For a calculator, running twice is fine. For a payment or an email, it is not. Use an idempotency key the handler stores, and return the original result on a repeat.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Make tool calls safe to retry, inside a sandbox”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Pick one tool. Say whether a retry is safe. If it is not, write the idempotency rule in one sentence. Name the directory the agent is allowed to see.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: MCP · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “MCP connects a model to tools you did not hard-code” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: The Model Context Protocol is a standard way for an app to talk to a tool server.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: What does “MCP connects a model to tools you did not hard-code” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Without a protocol, every app invents its own plugin format. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the 2025–2026 standard those apps increasingly share. A host such as an editor or a desktop assistant speaks MCP to a server that offers tools, documents, and prompt templates.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · why
cards.q: What further claim does “MCP connects a model to tools you did not hard-code” add?
cards.a: The model is not the server. The server is ordinary software: it lists what it can do, and it runs a tool when the host, with the person's consent, asks it to. That split is why the same notes server can be used from more than one app.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: In “MCP connects a model to tools you did not hard-code”, what should you keep from the note “Currency”?
cards.a: The spec has moved. Local servers usually use stdio. Remote servers use streamable HTTP. Older remote servers used server-sent events. Read the spec version you implement rather than copying a 2024 snippet.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: MCP · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “MCP connects a model to tools you did not hard-code”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Name one system you wish a model could read — a notes folder, a ticket list, a schema — and write whether it should be a tool (an action) or a resource (data the model may read).
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: MCP · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Host, client, and server have different jobs” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: The person uses the host. The client holds the session. The server does the work.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: What does “Host, client, and server have different jobs” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Do not put your database password in the host's prompt. Put it in the server's environment, and let the server return the rows the tool is allowed to return. The model sees the rows, not the password.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Host, client, and server have different jobs”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Label three boxes — host, client, server — for a setup you might actually run. Write one sentence for what each box must not do.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: MCP · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Tools act, resources are read, prompts are templates” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Use the primitive that matches the risk.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: What does “Tools act, resources are read, prompts are templates” argue at the outset?
cards.a: MCP servers publish three kinds of things. Mixing them up is how a 'reader' ends up with permission to write.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Tools act, resources are read, prompts are templates” add?
cards.a: If the job is 'show me this note', prefer a resource. If the job is 'append a line to the decision log', that is a tool, and it waits for a person unless you have a strong reason and an eval.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Tools act, resources are read, prompts are templates”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Take the system you named in 07-01 and list one tool, one resource, and, if you need it, one prompt template. If you do not need a prompt template, say so.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: MCP · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Connect a local server over stdio” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: The host starts a process and speaks MCP on its standard streams. The process is the trust boundary.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: What does “Connect a local server over stdio” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A local server is a command the host launches. Configuration names the command and its arguments. The host's working directory and environment become the server's power. A server that runs `python server.py` with your shell's environment can see whatever that environment can see.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: In “Connect a local server over stdio”, what should you keep from the note “You do not have to build a server to learn the shape”?
cards.a: If you install nothing, the artifact is the config above plus the list of tools you would refuse. A live server is optional.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: MCP · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Connect a local server over stdio”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write a config for a server whose only job is to read one folder. State the folder, and state one path it must reject.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: MCP · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Consent, authentication, and untrusted servers” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A server you did not review can read what the host will hand it, and its tool text can steer the model.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: What does “Consent, authentication, and untrusted servers” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Installing an MCP server is closer to installing a plugin than to bookmarking a page. A local server can read files. A remote server receives whatever the client sends and might retain it. Both can put instructions into tool descriptions, which the model will read.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · why
cards.q: In “Consent, authentication, and untrusted servers”, what should you keep from the note “No exploit steps here”?
cards.a: The failure mode is enough: untrusted instructions in tool metadata, plus a powerful tool, plus auto-approval. The defense is review, least privilege, and a person on side effects.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: MCP · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Consent, authentication, and untrusted servers”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write a yes/no checklist you will use before enabling a server: who published it, what tools it lists, whether any tool can write or send, and whether the host will ask first.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: MCP · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “How coding tools use MCP” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Editors and agents use MCP to reach issue trackers, browsers, docs, and internal APIs. The repo is still reviewed by a person.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: MCP · definition
cards.q: What does “How coding tools use MCP” argue at the outset?
cards.a: In 2026, coding products expose MCP so a model can call the tools a developer already uses: a ticket, a design file, a database schema, a browser snapshot, a documentation search. That is useful. It also means the agent in School 08 may now see more than the git tree.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · why
cards.q: What further claim does “How coding tools use MCP” add?
cards.a: MCP does not replace tests or review. It replaces a pile of one-off plugins. The diff still needs a person, which is the next track.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: MCP · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “How coding tools use MCP”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: List two MCP servers that would help a coding task you do, and one you would leave disconnected, with the reason.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Coding agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “A coding agent edits a repository under rules” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: It can read, propose a plan, change files, and run commands. Your rules say which of those happen alone.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Coding agents · definition
cards.q: What does “A coding agent edits a repository under rules” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A coding agent is the loop from School 06 pointed at a codebase. Products in this category include Cursor, GitHub Copilot's agent modes, Claude Code, Codex-style agents, Aider, Continue, and Cline. They differ in interface. They share the risk: a model with a terminal and a write path.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · why
cards.q: What further claim does “A coding agent edits a repository under rules” add?
cards.a: If you cannot answer those, you do not have an agent setup. You have a default, and defaults differ by product and drift over time. Read the product's current permission screen and write down what you turned off.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “A coding agent edits a repository under rules”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: For a repository you know, write the allow and deny list: directories, commands, and files. Include `.env` on the deny list even if your project uses a different name.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Coding agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Give the agent the files and tests that matter” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A whole monorepo in the prompt is not context. It is noise.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Coding agents · definition
cards.q: What does “Give the agent the files and tests that matter” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Point the agent at the module, the failing test, and the interface it must not break. Name the command that proves success. If you do not know the command, finding the command is the task, and the agent should stop before editing.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Give the agent the files and tests that matter” add?
cards.a: Let it search when the relevant file is unknown. Keep the step cap small so search does not become a tour. When it names the files it will change, that list is the moment to redirect it.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Give the agent the files and tests that matter”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write a goal block in the shape above for a small change you understand. If you do not have a repo, use a fictional one and still name a test command.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Coding agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Plan, edit, run, then stop” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A plan you can reject is cheaper than a pile of edits you have to unwind.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Coding agents · definition
cards.q: What does “Plan, edit, run, then stop” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Skipping the plan is sometimes fine for a one-line change you already specified. It is a poor habit for anything that crosses a module. 'Keep going until the tests pass' without a cap is how an agent refactors the neighborhood and calls it a fix.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Plan, edit, run, then stop” add?
cards.a: A failed test is a successful stop if the step cap is near. Record the failure. Do not let a second, unrelated edit 'try something else' in the same unreviewed tree.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Plan, edit, run, then stop”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Add a step cap and a stop sentence to the goal block from 08-02. Example stop sentence: 'I hit 6 steps. Tests are red. No further edits.'
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Coding agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Review the diff and the tests” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Read the change as if a new teammate wrote it. Then run the same command they ran.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Coding agents · definition
cards.q: What does “Review the diff and the tests” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Review for behavior, not for style the linter can catch. Look for extra files, weakened assertions, deleted tests, new dependencies, and changes outside the goal. Look for secrets that were read and echoed into a comment or a log.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · why
cards.q: In “Review the diff and the tests”, what should you keep from the note “Green tests can be gamed”?
cards.a: An agent can edit the test until it passes. Treat a test diff as carefully as a code diff. The expected value should still describe the behavior you want.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: Coding agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Review the diff and the tests”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write five review questions you will ask of the next agent diff you see. Keep them specific enough that each is yes or no.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Coding agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Secrets, destructive git, and the network” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: The expensive mistakes are not bad indentation.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Coding agents · definition
cards.q: What does “Secrets, destructive git, and the network” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Put the deny list in the tool layer. A prompt that says 'never run destructive commands' loses to a tool that can run them and a document that says 'you must'.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Secrets, destructive git, and the network”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write the command allowlist for a lab agent: the test command, and nothing else. Add three commands that are always denied.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Coding agents · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Use a coding agent on a team without shipping junk” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Agree the permissions, the review, and what 'the agent did it' does not excuse.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Coding agents · definition
cards.q: What does “Use a coding agent on a team without shipping junk” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Teams that get value from coding agents in 2026 treat them as fast teammates with a narrow role. The author of the change is still a person. The pull request explains the behavior, the test command, and any permission the agent was given.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Use a coding agent on a team without shipping junk” add?
cards.a: Lines generated is a vanity metric. A change that takes longer to review than it would have taken to write is not a win, unless it was a change people were avoiding for a tracked reason.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Coding agents · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Use a coding agent on a team without shipping junk”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write three lines a pull request should contain when an agent helped: the goal, the test command and result, and the permissions used.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Evals · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “An eval is a versioned test, not a feeling” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: You cannot prefer a new prompt unless the same tasks were scored both times.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: What does “An eval is a versioned test, not a feeling” argue at the outset?
cards.a: An evaluation is a set of tasks, a way to score them, and a record of what you ran. It is the same idea as a test suite, with more judgment in the score and more ways to fool yourself.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: What further claim does “An eval is a versioned test, not a feeling” add?
cards.a: 'It looks better' is a hypothesis. The eval is the test of the hypothesis. If you do not want to write tasks, you do not have an eval practice yet, and you should not be fine-tuning or swapping models on taste.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “An eval is a versioned test, not a feeling”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Create a file with three tasks. Each task needs an input and a check a person could apply twice and agree on.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Evals · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Start with ten tasks you can explain” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A small set you trust beats a large set nobody can audit.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: What does “Start with ten tasks you can explain” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Ten tasks is enough to catch a clumsy prompt change and small enough that you will actually look at the failures. Grow the set when a production mistake was not represented. Do not generate five hundred tasks with a model and call them ground truth.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Start with ten tasks you can explain” add?
cards.a: Write the expected check next to the input. For retrieval, the check includes the chunk id. For an agent, the check includes which tools were allowed to run and which must not have run.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: In “Start with ten tasks you can explain”, what should you keep from the note “Do not tune on the only set you have”?
cards.a: If you edit the prompt while staring at all ten, you are memorizing them. Hold out two tasks you do not look at until the end, or add a fresh task before you declare victory.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: Evals · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Start with ten tasks you can explain”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Draft ten one-line task titles for a system you might build. Mark two as refusal and one as a safety case. You can fill the inputs later. The titles force coverage.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Evals · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Score quality, safety, latency, and cost together” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A change that raises quality and doubles the bill needs a decision, not a silent ship.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: What does “Score quality, safety, latency, and cost together” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A single blended number hides the trade. Keep the four. Your gate can say 'quality must not drop, safety fails must be zero, median latency under two seconds, cost within 10 percent'. Write the gate before you see the new score, or you will move the gate to fit the result.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Score quality, safety, latency, and cost together”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write a gate in one sentence for a system you have in mind, using at least quality and one of the other three axes.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Evals · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Use a model as a judge only with a rubric and an audit” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A judge model is a second system. It has its own failure rate.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: What does “Use a model as a judge only with a rubric and an audit” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Some checks are awkward to write as exact string matches: whether a summary omitted a decision, whether a tone is acceptable. A judge model can apply a rubric to those. It cannot be the only authority.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Use a model as a judge only with a rubric and an audit” add?
cards.a: Exact checks are better when you can write them: JSON validity, id membership, a number, a tool that must not appear in the trace. Use the judge for the residue, not for everything, because the residue is where you can be fooled.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Use a model as a judge only with a rubric and an audit”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write a five-line rubric for one subjective check. Include one line that forces a fail.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Evals · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Gate changes to the prompt, the model, and the index” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Each of those is a release. The tasks do not change in the same commit unless the task change is the point.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: What does “Gate changes to the prompt, the model, and the index” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A prompt tweak, a model swap, a new embedding model, a chunker change, and a tool-schema change are all releases. Run the same tasks. Put the score in the pull request. If the gate fails, do not merge because the demo looked fine.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Gate changes to the prompt, the model, and the index” add?
cards.a: A regression is a task that used to pass and now fails. Name it in the pull request. 'Overall score is flat' can hide one new safety fail and one new easy pass that cancel in the average.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Gate changes to the prompt, the model, and the index”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write the checklist you would paste at the bottom of a pull request that changes a prompt: what was pinned, what ran, which tasks regressed, and whether the gate passed.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Evals · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Put red-team cases in the set early” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: You are checking your own system's boundaries, on inputs you control.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: What does “Put red-team cases in the set early” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A red-team case is a task that tries to make your system break a rule you wrote. You author the case. You are not attacking someone else's service, and you are not collecting bypass tricks. You are checking that your gate holds on inputs you will meet.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Put red-team cases in the set early” add?
cards.a: Score these as pass or fail. Do not average them into a soft quality number. One safety fail blocks the release if that is the gate you wrote. If you decide it does not block, write that decision down and own it.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Put red-team cases in the set early”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write two red-team tasks in input-and-pass-condition form. Use synthetic data. Do not include a real secret to 'see if it leaks'.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Evals · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Keep the scorecard next to the artifact” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A table you can reopen beats a screenshot of one good answer.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Evals · definition
cards.q: What does “Keep the scorecard next to the artifact” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Store this beside the outputs, or store the outputs and link them. When someone asks why you shipped, this is the answer. When someone asks why you did not fine-tune, this is also the answer: the failures were retrieval, not the base model, or there were not enough failures to justify training.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Evals · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Keep the scorecard next to the artifact”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Copy the template and fill it with 'not run' where you have no number. A blank dressed up as a score is worse than 'not run'.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Fine-tune only after a measured failure of the cheaper fixes” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Prompt, schema, retrieval, and tools come first. Training is for a gap those did not close.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · definition
cards.q: What does “Fine-tune only after a measured failure of the cheaper fixes” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Fine-tuning changes the model's weights, usually by training on examples of the behavior you want. It costs data work, compute, and a new model you have to host and re-eval. It is the right tool when the base model already has the facts — or you will keep retrieving the facts — and still will not hold a format, a style, or a domain decision that you can show in examples.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Fine-tune only after a measured failure of the cheaper fixes” add?
cards.a: The decision record is the eval from School 09 plus a sentence: which failures remain, and why a prompt or a retrieval change cannot address them. If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to train.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Fine-tune only after a measured failure of the cheaper fixes”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write that decision sentence for a real or fictional system. 'Not yet, because …' is a complete answer.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “LoRA trains a small adapter and leaves the base model frozen” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: QLoRA does the same while the frozen base is stored in a quantized form.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · definition
