cards.q: What does “LoRA trains a small adapter and leaves the base model frozen” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Full fine-tuning updates every weight. That is expensive and easy to damage. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes the base model and trains small matrices that sit alongside certain layers. You store the adapter, not a full second copy of the model. At inference you load the base plus the adapter.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · why
cards.q: What further claim does “LoRA trains a small adapter and leaves the base model frozen” add?
cards.a: QLoRA quantizes that frozen base so the training job fits on a smaller GPU. The adapter is still what you train. People say 'I quantized' when they mean 'I fine-tuned' and the reverse. In a design review, say which one you did.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · definition
cards.q: What does “LoRA trains a small adapter and leaves the base model frozen” add after those claims?
cards.a: Preference methods such as DPO train from pairs of better and worse answers. They are a fit when the issue is which output a person prefers, and a poor fit when the issue is a missing document. You still need a base that can produce the better answer often enough to learn from.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · definition
cards.q: In “LoRA trains a small adapter and leaves the base model frozen”, what should you keep from the note “Tools you will see named”?
cards.a: Hugging Face PEFT, Axolotl, Unsloth, and the hosted fine-tuning APIs from the major labs. The method matters more than the brand: frozen base, small adapter, same eval before and after.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “LoRA trains a small adapter and leaves the base model frozen”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: In three sentences, explain to a teammate the difference between quantizing a model to run it and training a LoRA adapter on it.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Training data has a format, a license, and a leakage problem” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Examples teach the behavior. They also teach secrets you forgot were in the log.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · definition
cards.q: What does “Training data has a format, a license, and a leakage problem” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A typical supervised set is a list of conversations or instruction pairs: the input the model will see, and the output you want. The format must match how you will call the model later. Training on essays and then calling the model as a JSON API is a self-inflicted miss.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · why
cards.q: In “Training data has a format, a license, and a leakage problem”, what should you keep from the note “Synthetic data”?
cards.a: Data a model wrote is allowed only if you review it and you are allowed to use it. It repeats the teacher's mistakes at scale. A person still owns the guidelines.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Training data has a format, a license, and a leakage problem”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Describe the columns of a training row for one task. Add a column for the source of the row and a yes/no for 'contains personal data'. That yes/no must be no before the row is usable.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Compare the adapter to the base model on the same tasks” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Keep the adapter only if the scorecard says so, including the tasks that used to pass.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · definition
cards.q: What does “Compare the adapter to the base model on the same tasks” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Run the School 09 tasks twice: base model, then base plus adapter. Same prompts, same retrieval, same tools. The adapter wins only if the failures you trained for improved and the safety tasks did not get worse.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Compare the adapter to the base model on the same tasks” add?
cards.a: Watch for a model that learned the training phrasing and now refuses to answer a valid variant. That shows up as regressions on tasks that used to pass. It is the usual cost of a small, narrow set.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Compare the adapter to the base model on the same tasks”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write the comparison header: task, base result, adapter result, regression yes/no. Fill it with the decision you expect, and note which safety task would make you throw the adapter away.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Prefer a prompt or a tool when that is the whole gap” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Most 'we should fine-tune' reviews end with a schema, a retrieval fix, or a smaller model.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · definition
cards.q: What does “Prefer a prompt or a tool when that is the whole gap” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Walk this list before you spend on training.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Prefer a prompt or a tool when that is the whole gap” add?
cards.a: This is the judgment hiring panels are probing when they ask 'how do you decide to fine-tune'. The answer is a sequence of measured exclusions, not enthusiasm for training.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Prefer a prompt or a tool when that is the whole gap”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Take the decision sentence from 10-01 and run it down this list. Stop at the first item that applies.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Hu et al., 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685.

cards.title: Safety · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Write a one-page safety policy” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Name the data, the tools, the actions that need a person, and what you will not build.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Safety · definition
cards.q: What does “Write a one-page safety policy” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A policy you can apply is one page. A policy that quotes every guideline and changes nothing is not a control.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Write a one-page safety policy” add?
cards.a: Fill it for the capstone before you connect a tool. If a line is 'not sure', the tool stays disconnected. Update the page when the system changes, in the same change as the tool list.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Write a one-page safety policy”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Fill the six lines. Use 'none yet' where that is true.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Safety · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Decide retention before you log the prompt” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Prompts are often personal data. A debug log is a database.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Safety · definition
cards.q: What does “Decide retention before you log the prompt” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A prompt can contain a person's name, a health note, a customer message, or a secret. The provider's retention setting and your own log are two different stores. Configure both. 'The vendor probably deletes it' is not a setting.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Decide retention before you log the prompt” add?
cards.a: Synthetic fixtures belong in the repo. Real prompts do not, unless the repo is private and approved for that data. This course's exercises use synthetic fixtures for that reason.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Decide retention before you log the prompt”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Add two lines to your policy page: how long traces live, and what you will redact before a trace is written.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Safety · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “A person approves sends, payments, and deletes” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Drafting is not the same action as doing.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Safety · definition
cards.q: What does “A person approves sends, payments, and deletes” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Let the system draft the email, the refund, the shell command, or the pull request. Show the draft and the arguments. A person confirms. The tool layer checks that the confirmation matches those arguments. If the model changes the arguments after the yes, the yes is void.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · why
cards.q: What further claim does “A person approves sends, payments, and deletes” add?
cards.a: Unattended action is a product decision with a name, a kill switch, and an eval. It is not the default because a demo was smoother without the click.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “A person approves sends, payments, and deletes”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Mark each of the four rows for your capstone: will you stop at draft, or do you have a named reason to go further? 'The demo' is not a reason.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Safety · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Write an incident note when the model misbehaves” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A short note beats a thread of screenshots.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Safety · definition
cards.q: What does “Write an incident note when the model misbehaves” argue at the outset?
cards.a: If a tool acted, contain that first: revoke the key, disable the server, rotate the secret. Then write the note. An incident without a new eval task will return as a surprise.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Write an incident note when the model misbehaves”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Fill the template for a fictional incident: a retrieved page told the model to approve a refund, and the draft looked convincing. Say whether a tool acted. In a well-built system, it did not.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Safety · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “What this course will not help you do” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: The boundary is part of the teaching.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Safety · definition
cards.q: What does “What this course will not help you do” argue at the outset?
cards.a: This campus will not help you write malware, hide a prompt injection, bypass a provider's safety stack, scrape a system you are not allowed to access, or automate harm. Those are not advanced modules. They are out of scope.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · why
cards.q: What further claim does “What this course will not help you do” add?
cards.a: It will also not certify you, grant you a model, or guarantee a job. The artifact you leave with is a capstone you can explain: what it calls, what it refuses, and how you scored it.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Safety · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “What this course will not help you do”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Add a 'will not build' line to your policy page that is specific to your domain, not a copy of this lesson's first sentence.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Product skills · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Name the job before you name the model” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A product sentence has a person, a job, and a constraint. The model is an implementation choice.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: What does “Name the job before you name the model” argue at the outset?
cards.a: Hiring posts for AI product managers in 2026 ask for the same discipline as the engineering tracks: a user, a workflow, a measurement, and a risk. Start with the job-to-be-done.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Name the job before you name the model” add?
cards.a: If you cannot fill those clauses, you do not have a feature. You have a model in search of a demo. The citation requirement is what makes this a retrieval product. The minute is a latency budget. The handbook staying put is a privacy requirement. The model choice comes after.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Name the job before you name the model”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write a four-line job statement for something you would actually use. Include a latency or cost constraint and a proof constraint, such as a citation or a test.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Product skills · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Write a one-page spec” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Problem, user, non-goals, success, risks, and the first milestone.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: What does “Write a one-page spec” argue at the outset?
cards.a: One page forces the cut. A ten-page spec that does not name a non-goal will be read as permission to build the platform.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Write a one-page spec”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Fill the six sections in short lines for your job statement. If success has no number or no pass/fail, it is not success yet.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Product skills · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Share four numbers with engineering” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Quality, safety fails, latency, and cost per successful task.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: What does “Share four numbers with engineering” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A roadmap slide that says 'improve AI quality' does not tell an engineer what to do. The shared numbers do. They are the same four axes as the eval gate, expressed as a product promise.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Share four numbers with engineering” add?
cards.a: Add a counter-metric so the team cannot game the first number. If you only score deflection, the system will refuse hard tickets and look successful. Pair deflection with a check that the citation was real, or with a sample a person reviews.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Share four numbers with engineering”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write the four numbers for your spec, plus one counter-metric. Use targets you could measure this month, not a press-release percentage.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Product skills · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Design the empty, slow, wrong, and unsafe states” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: The model will hit all four. The interface should say what happened.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: What does “Design the empty, slow, wrong, and unsafe states” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A chat box with no states is a demo. A product names these four and logs them. The unsafe state is especially easy to get wrong: a coy message that hints at the blocked action teaches the next try.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Design the empty, slow, wrong, and unsafe states”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write the four messages in your product's voice, each in one sentence. Read the unsafe message and delete any hint of a workaround.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Product skills · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Ship a prototype, then an eval, then a limited release” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A limited release has a named audience, a kill switch, and a date you will read the scorecard.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: What does “Ship a prototype, then an eval, then a limited release” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A kill switch is a flag that disables the model path and leaves the previous workflow intact. If there is no previous workflow, the kill switch is 'stop showing the feature'. Shipping without that flag means an incident becomes a scramble.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: In “Ship a prototype, then an eval, then a limited release”, what should you keep from the note “Buy versus build”?
cards.a: A hosted agent product can be the right milestone if it meets the policy page. You still own the eval and the data question. Buying the UI does not buy the judgment.
cards.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

cards.title: Product skills · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Ship a prototype, then an eval, then a limited release”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write the audience for a limited release in one sentence, the kill switch, and the date you will read the numbers.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Product skills · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Add voice only when latency and handoff are designed” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Speech recognition and speech synthesis are models with their own failure modes. They do not replace the eval.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Product skills · definition
cards.q: What does “Add voice only when latency and handoff are designed” argue at the outset?
cards.a: A voice interface adds two models and a clock. Speech-to-text can drop names, numbers, and domain words. Text-to-speech can say a wrong answer smoothly, which is worse than a wrong paragraph the person can skim. Barge-in, silence, and background noise are product states, not polish.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Add voice only when latency and handoff are designed” add?
cards.a: If your background is phone systems, bring that operational care to the latency budget and the handoff. Leave the vendor-specific telephony course for a telephony course. Here, voice is an interface on top of the same retrieval, tools, and evals.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Product skills · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Add voice only when latency and handoff are designed”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Decide whether your spec needs voice in the first release. If yes, write the latency budget and the handoff sentence. If no, write it as a non-goal.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cards.title: Capstone · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “Choose a capstone you can finish on your own notes” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: A folder you are allowed to use, questions you wrote, citations, and one read-only tool.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · definition
cards.q: What does “Choose a capstone you can finish on your own notes” argue at the outset?
cards.a: The capstone is a small grounded assistant over a corpus you control: ten to thirty notes, a handbook chapter, or a public spec you have the right to copy into a lab folder. It answers questions from that corpus, cites chunk ids, and refuses when the corpus is silent.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · why
cards.q: What further claim does “Choose a capstone you can finish on your own notes” add?
cards.a: A capstone that needs a team, a budget, and a month of data cleaning is a job, not this exercise. Cut it until you can demo it in one sitting.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · scenario
cards.q: You sit down to practice “Choose a capstone you can finish on your own notes”. What should you produce before you move on?
cards.a: Write the corpus path, the user, and the one tool. If you have no corpus, create five synthetic notes and use those. Synthetic is allowed. Someone else's private data is not.
cards.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

cite.title: Lewis et al., 2020. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2005.11401.

cards.title: Capstone · interview

cards.q: An interviewer asks what “How do you decide to fine-tune?” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?

cards.title: Interview practice · definition
cards.q: What does “How do you decide to fine-tune?” argue at the outset?
cards.a: I fine-tune only after a fixed task set shows that the schema, the prompt, retrieval, and tools still leave a behavior I can teach with examples. Facts that change stay in retrieval. I keep the adapter only if it beats the base model on that set without new safety failures.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Interview practice · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “How do you evaluate a prompt or model change?” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?

cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Interview practice · definition
cards.q: What does “How do you evaluate a prompt or model change?” argue at the outset?
cards.a: I keep a versioned task set and score quality, safety, latency, and cost. I pin the prompt, model id, and index. I compare to the last baseline and block the change if a safety task regresses or the gate I wrote in advance fails.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Interview practice · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “How do you stop an agent from doing damage?” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?

cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Interview practice · definition
cards.q: What does “How do you stop an agent from doing damage?” argue at the outset?
cards.a: The agent can call only named tools. Arguments have to match the schema before the handler runs. Read-only tools stay inside a step and spend cap. Sending, paying, deleting, and pushing wait for a person who sees the exact arguments. The trace is what I review, not the summary.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Interview practice · interview

cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Interview practice · definition
cards.q: What does “What is MCP, and when would you use it?” argue at the outset?
cards.a: MCP lets a host's client talk to a server that exposes tools, resources, and prompts over stdio locally or HTTP remotely. I use it when I want a reviewed server — notes, tickets, docs — available to an assistant without inventing a plugin format. I do not enable a server I have not read, and I do not auto-approve write tools.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Interview practice · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “How do you review a coding agent's change?” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Read the diff, rerun the tests, and reject hunks that do not serve the goal.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Interview practice · definition
cards.q: What does “How do you review a coding agent's change?” argue at the outset?
cards.a: I look at the diff as a teammate's change: extra files, weakened tests, new dependencies, and anything outside the goal. I run the test command myself and read the output. Secrets, push, and unrestricted shell are denied in the tool layer. The person who merges is responsible.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Interview practice · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “How do you control cost and latency?” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: Smaller context, a cheaper model where the eval allows it, caps, and cost per successful task.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Interview practice · definition
cards.q: What does “How do you control cost and latency?” argue at the outset?
cards.a: I retrieve passages instead of pasting the corpus, cap output tokens, and route easy rows to a smaller model only when those rows pass the same checks. I set timeouts and backoff. I report cost per successful task, not per call, and I read the provider's current prices rather than a memorized rate.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Interview practice · interview
cards.q: An interviewer asks what “How do you know a grounded answer is not invented?” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
cards.a: The citation has to be an id you retrieved, and some tasks must refuse.
cards.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

cards.title: Interview practice · definition
cards.q: What does “How do you know a grounded answer is not invented?” argue at the outset?
cards.a: I score retrieval separately: did the right chunk id appear. The answer may cite only ids that were retrieved, and the code drops the rest. The task set includes questions the corpus cannot answer, where refusal is the pass. A fluent paragraph with a made-up bibliography fails.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.title: Interview practice · interview

cards.title: Interview practice · definition
cards.q: What does “What goes in an AI product spec?” argue at the outset?
cards.a: I write the person's job before the model name, including what this version will not do. Success is quality, safety, latency, and cost per successful task, plus a counter-metric so the team cannot game one number. Empty, slow, wrong, and unsafe states are specified. A limited release has an audience and a way to turn the model path off.
cards.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

cards.q: What should the bot have done when the passage did not contain a 90-day window?

cards.q: Which log line belongs on this incident?
cards.a: Retrieved passage, claim, and whether the passage contains the claim.

cards.q: What do you change before this bot answers another refund question?
cards.a: Generate only from a passage that contains the claim, and refuse when none does.
cards.why: That is the retrieval split: fetch, check, then speak.

cards.title: Agents · scenario
cards.q: What is the note, in this loop?
cards.a: Data the model read. It is not a new system instruction and not an approval.
cards.why: Instructions inside retrieved text are a known way to steer a model that treats them as orders.

cards.title: Agents · scenario
cards.q: Who is allowed to decide that the send runs?
cards.a: Your code, using the allow-list. The model only proposed the call.
cards.why: A proposal is not a side effect. The host runs the call or it does not.

cards.title: Agents · scenario
cards.q: The send tool is not on the allow-list. What happens next?
cards.a: The call does not run, and the trace says the tool was denied.
cards.why: Denial is a successful safety outcome. The loop should stop or ask a person.

cards.title: Agents · scenario
cards.q: Which cap belongs on this loop even if a later note says to keep going?
cards.a: A fixed step cap that stops new calls after the budget.
cards.why: An uncapped loop will follow the next note that says to continue.

cards.title: MCP · scenario
cards.q: What did tools/list actually prove?
cards.a: The server advertised a name and a schema. It did not prove the user wants that side effect.
cards.why: Discovery and consent are different steps in the host.

cards.title: MCP · scenario
cards.q: The model’s tools/call arguments match the schema. What is still missing?
cards.a: A host decision to allow that tool for this user and this task.
cards.why: A valid envelope can still be the wrong action.

cards.title: MCP · scenario
cards.q: Where does that decision live?
cards.a: In the host, before the side effect. Not inside the server’s advertisement.
cards.why: The server cannot be the party that grants itself a send.

cards.title: MCP · scenario
cards.q: What should the trace show if you refuse?
cards.a: initialize, tools/list, the proposed tools/call, and a host denial before any send.
cards.why: The teaching inspector is a picture of that order. A real host keeps the same order.

cards.title: Coding agents · scenario
cards.q: What is missing from the “tests passed” sentence?
cards.a: The command that ran and the output a person can read.
cards.why: A summary is not a log. The artifact is the output.

cards.title: Coding agents · scenario
cards.q: What do you do with the config edit?
cards.a: Keep it out of this merge unless a task names that file.
cards.why: Edits outside the plan are a new task, not a bonus.

cards.title: Coding agents · scenario
cards.q: Who merges?
cards.a: A person who has read the diff and the test log.
cards.why: The agent can prepare the change. It is not the reviewer.

cards.title: Coding agents · scenario
cards.q: What do you tell the agent to do next?
cards.a: Drop the unnamed file, attach the test output, and wait.
cards.why: The loop stops at the human gate. It does not retry the merge in the same breath.

cards.title: Evals · scenario
cards.q: Which number blocks the ship?
cards.a: Safety failures rose against the baseline.
cards.why: The gate is all four checks. A gain in quality does not buy a safety regression.

cards.title: Evals · scenario
cards.q: Why is the demo not enough?
cards.a: The demo is one example. The score is the versioned set.
cards.why: People remember the example that worked.

cards.title: Evals · scenario
cards.q: Someone proposes editing the set so the new prompt’s misses are removed. What do you do?
cards.a: Refuse. Score both prompts on the version that was already agreed.
cards.why: Changing the set after the result makes the comparison void.

cards.title: Evals · scenario
cards.q: What does the review keep attached to the decision?
cards.a: The scorecard for quality, safety, latency, and cost, next to the demo.
cards.why: The decision is the card, not the memory of the meeting.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · scenario
cards.q: What should have been tried before the training job?
cards.a: The prompt, the output shape, and retrieval of the policy line that is already indexed.
cards.why: Training is the expensive fix. A miss you can retrieve is not a weight problem yet.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · scenario
cards.q: Training loss fell. What does that not show?
cards.a: That the adapter beats the base model on held-out tasks.
cards.why: Loss is on the rows you trained. The tasks are the decision.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · scenario
cards.q: Why is doubling the rank not the next automatic step?
cards.a: Rank is a budget of trainable numbers. More rank can memorize the miss instead of fixing the pipeline.
cards.why: A higher rank is not a quality setting.

cards.title: Fine-tuning · scenario
cards.q: What comparison do you require before keeping the adapter?
cards.a: The adapter and the base model on the same versioned tasks.
cards.why: Keep the adapter only if that comparison says it won without a safety regression.

cards.title: APIs and cost · scenario
cards.q: What do you do with the key first?
cards.a: Remove it from the page, rotate it, and call the model from a server you control.
cards.why: A key that shipped in a script is already copied.

cards.title: APIs and cost · scenario
cards.q: Why did the customer get two orders?
cards.a: The retry repeated a side effect that was not safe to run twice.
cards.why: A timeout does not prove the first call failed.

cards.title: APIs and cost · scenario
cards.q: What should the client send on the second attempt?
cards.a: The same idempotency key, so the server can recognize the repeat.
cards.why: Reads can retry more freely. An order cannot.

cards.title: APIs and cost · scenario
cards.q: How do you explain the token spike?
cards.a: Count tokens in, tokens out, and the retries. The nicer prompt is not the first suspect.
cards.why: The bill is those counts. A spike without them is a guess.

cards.title: Safety · scenario
cards.q: What should the policy have done before the paste?
cards.a: Named that record as data that does not go into a prompt.
cards.why: A policy you apply after the paste is a postmortem, not a control.

cards.title: Safety · scenario
cards.q: The draft is excellent. Why is send still blocked?
cards.a: Sending waits for a person. A finished draft is not an approval.
cards.why: The side effect is the send, not the writing.

cards.title: Safety · scenario
cards.q: What do you do about the account number that already left?
cards.a: Treat it as exposed: rotate or protect what you can, and keep it out of the next retry.
cards.why: Redacting the screen does not pull the log back.

cards.title: Safety · scenario
cards.q: How should a later refund draft get the account facts?
cards.a: From a tool that reads the record outside the prompt, with a person on the send.
cards.why: The model can draft from a minimum. The secret stays in the system that already holds it.
